title: In most programming languages, 0.1 + 0.2 doesn’t equal 0.3
body: Type 0.1 + 0.2 into JavaScript or Python and you get 0.30000000000000004. Computers usually store decimals as binary floating-point numbers, defined by the IEEE 754 standard, and just as 1/3 never ends in decimal, 0.1 never ends in binary. The machine keeps the nearest value it can fit, and the tiny rounding errors become visible when numbers are added.

slides.heading: Why 0.1 is hard
slides.text: In binary, 0.1 is 0.0001100110011… repeating forever. A standard 64-bit number keeps about 15 to 17 significant decimal digits, then rounds the rest.

slides.heading: Usually harmless
slides.text: The error is around one part in ten quadrillion, too small to matter for most science or graphics. It bites when code checks whether two results are exactly equal.

slides.heading: How money is handled
slides.text: Financial software often counts whole cents as integers or uses special decimal number types, so adding up prices stays exact.

slides.question: Why can’t a computer store 0.1 exactly?
slides.explanation: Just as 1/3 never ends in decimal, 0.1 never ends in binary. The machine keeps the nearest value it can fit, and the rounding errors show up when numbers are added.
